proposals.relationship: Cook uses Harris’s account of provinces replacing local settlements and amorphous regions to support his challenge to regionalism as a historical unit of analysis.
proposals.evidence_note: Own complete 1983 review:138 and 141, quoting and interpreting Harris’s chapter in Heartland and Hinterland. Cook praises its insight while saying it is not an adequate editorial conclusion; its provincial argument helps him draw a conclusion that may contradict the volume’s organizing assumptions. This is Cook’s substantive use of Harris, not a new reading of the original chapter or wholesale rejection of regional research. Existing field critique edge_944 remains unchanged.

proposals.relationship: Cook invokes Berger’s history of English-Canadian historical writing to frame the displacement and reassessment of the national school.
proposals.evidence_note: Own complete 1983 review:137 characterizes The Writing of Canadian History (1976) as an epitaph that recognizes both accomplishments and failings and points toward new questions and synthesis. This is a bounded historiographical resource within Cook’s regionalism argument, not formal teaching or adoption of every judgment in Berger’s unread book. The national-tradition group critique retains its wider joint context.

proposals.relationship: Cook credits McKay’s account of wartime Atlantic Canada with prompting reconsideration of the region’s place in the transformation of early twentieth-century Canada.
proposals.evidence_note: Own complete 1993 review:149–150 treats McKay’s synthesis of social, economic, cultural and political history, the Halifax Explosion and postwar labour conflict; Cook pairs this with Howell’s chapter when urging broader reconsideration. The resource is particular to these chapters and keeps Howell’s shared credit. McKay’s original chapter and later books are unread; praise does not prove agreement with every later McKay project.
primary_locators: The New History of Atlantic Canada (1993):149–150

proposals.relationship: Wright reports that Cook credited Creighton’s encouragement and exacting standards during his doctoral research on J. W. Dafoe.
proposals.evidence_note: Named substantive scholar Donald Wright’s original 2016 remembrance, paragraph beginning “At Toronto”, identifies the supervision and quotes Cook’s 1963 acknowledgment. Their disagreements about French Canada and continuing friendship remain explicit; this supports a particular scholarly-training contribution, not adoption of Creighton’s nationalism. The original 1963 acknowledgment and thesis were not independently read. Wright’s 2017 chapter opening independently identifies the supervisor but mainly studies earlier formation.

proposals.relationship: Wright reports Kealey’s acknowledgment of Cook’s early influence and their continuing intellectual exchange about the socialist journalist Phillips Thompson.
proposals.evidence_note: Named substantive scholar Donald Wright’s original 2016 remembrance, paragraphs beginning “He wrote a new introduction” and “Their many conversations”, distinguishes Kealey’s 1966 teaching encounter from later conversations and their joking Jimuel Briggs Society. This is a specific reported teaching and research exchange, not a claim that Cook supplied all of Kealey’s labour-history method or that later disagreements disappeared. Kealey’s original reminiscence and their correspondence remain unread.
primary_locators: Wright2016:two paragraphs beginning “He wrote a new introduction” and “Their many conversations”
